IN THE HIGH COURT OF KERALA AT ERNAKULAM
 PRESENT
 THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE A.MUHAMED MUSTAQUE
 &
 THE HONOURABLE DR. JUSTICE KAUSER EDAPPAGATH
FRIDAY, THE 19TH DAY OF NOVEMBER 2021 / 28TH KARTHIKA, 1943
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 AGAINST THE ORDER/JUDGMENT IN OP 1692/2012 OF FAMILY
 COURT,ERNAKULAM, ERNAKULAM
APPELLANT/S:

 'X'
 BY ADVS.
 SRI.C.M.NAZAR
 SRI.G.CHANDRASEKHAR
 SMT.K.BINDU RANI


RESPONDENT/S:

 'Y'
 BY ADVS.
 SRI.BOBY MATHEW
 SMT.K.MEERA


 THIS MATRIMONIAL APPEAL HAVING BEING FINALLY
HEARD ON 15/09/2021, THE COURT ON 19.11.2021 DELIVERED
THE FOLLOWING:
 "C.R."


 A.MUHAMED MUSTAQUE & DR.KAUSER EDAPPAGATH, JJ.

 ------------------------------------------
 Mat.Appeal No.434 of 2016
 ------------------------------------------

 J U D G M E N T

Dated this the 19th day of November, 2021

A.Muhamed Mustaque, J.

"People are always good company when they are doing what
they really enjoy." Samuel Butler (1)


 When marriage is in trouble due to inherent

incompatibility, enjoyment vanishes and what left in the

marriage is often confounding the Court. The troubled marriage

never ends happily; it gets worsened when one party moves the

Court. Here is a case of divorce of the parties who are living

separately since 2003.

2. A case for divorce on the ground of 'desertion' moved

by the husband ended in dismissal with scathing remarks about

1) Considerations of the decline of Italian Art [See: Delphi Complete Works of Samuel Butler (Illustrated)] (Series Five
Book 19) Kindle Edition]
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:3:-

his conduct and life style. He, accordingly, approached this

Court in this appeal. The parties are Christian by faith. Their

marriage was solemnized in accordance with the Christian rites

on 26.12.1994. Two daughters born in the wedlock in the year

1997 and 1999 respectively, have attained majority and they are

looking forward to lead a quiet and steady life. When we looked

into the case, we thought on assigning ordinary meaning to

'desertion'; the Family Court was justified in dismissing the

petition for divorce. However, on a deeper consideration of the

law, we are of the view that a glaring misunderstanding on the

point of law had resulted in dismissal. We looked at the true

meaning of 'desertion' in the context of divorce under Divorce

Act, 1869 . We find 'desertion' also mean refusal of a spouse to

'cohabit' even if such spouse has no intention to abandon the

marriage. Before venturing to the above exercise, we deem to

refer the brief factual situation.

MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:4:-

3. The appellant-husband is a retired Navy Officer. His

marriage with the respondent was an arranged marriage. The

appellant asserts that the initial phase of marriage was a happy

one; they lived together in different places in Kochi; then he

availed study leave for two years from August 2001 to 2003 to

obtain M.Tech and MBA degrees from US. The appellant states

that he returned to India in July, 2003. Thereafter, his attempt to

resume cohabitation did not yield any positive response. We will

advert to the evidence in the later part of this judgment. Since

the appellant assumed that the respondent abandoned

matrimonial relationship, he filed a petition for divorce before

the Family Court, Ernakulam, on the ground of desertion. The

petition for divorce was filed on 24.09.2012.

4. The respondent-wife had a different story to tell.

According to the respondent, the appellant never provided any

emotional or familial security and he was more pre-occupied in
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:5:-

forming various romantic internet alliances using multiple

identical aliases. It is further contended that the appellant was

more interested to lead a bachelor life without any family

responsibility. She pointed out that she and her children were

completely neglected. She also stated that she was compelled to

single handedly perform social and domestic chores including

medical, schooling and recreational needs of the children. It is

stated by her that her parents being convinced of neglect, forced

to take the children along with her to Bangalore in the year

2001. The defense of the wife clearly would show that there was

no emotional bonding between the parties ever since the

marriage and disillusionment with husband made her to stay

away from him. May be the appellant-husband herein is the

real defaulter when looked from the point of social mores. In the

context of Divorce Act , the Court has to consider whether such

refusal would amount to desertion or not.

MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:6:-

5. Let us examine the evidence. PW1 is the appellant.

He narrated his attempt to resume marital life. He deposed that

since August, 2001, there was no husband and wife relationship.

PW2 is the father of the appellant. He deposed about the

attempts made on his side to persuade the parties to live

together. He also stated that he tried to involve Fr. M Austin to

make efforts for reunion. He also stated that the joint counseling

arranged by Fr. Austin and Fr. Kandathil could not be conducted

as the respondent refused to turn up for the session. PW3 is the

uncle of the appellant. He deposed that he and his wife went

thrice to the residence of the respondent and held extensive

discussion to resolve the marital issues between the appellant

and the respondent. However, it is stated by him that due to

refusal on the side of the respondent-wife, both parties could not

resume cohabitation. Ext.A1 is the lawyer notice proceeded from

the side of the appellant dated 23.7.2004 requesting the
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:7:-

respondent to resume cohabitation. Ext.A2 is another lawyer

notice dated 16.8.2004 sent to the lawyer of the respondent. In

that, the appellant expressed his willingness to preserve the

marriage and to resume the marital relationship. Ext.A3 is the

report of the Consultant Psychiatrist, dated 30.11.2011. In that

report, it is stated that the parties are emotionally incompatible

for a normal marital life. Ext.A4 is the report of a private

Mediator. In the report, the Mediator stated that the attempt to

settle the issues to facilitate reunion failed and there exists little

chance for reunion. We are not referring to other documents

produced on the side of the appellant. This may not have much

relevance for consideration on the point of law involved in this

case.

6. On the side of the respondent, she was examined as

RW1 and Ext.B1 was marked as documentary evidence. The

case as projected by her is that the appellant refused to accept
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:8:-

the realities and situation in life. According to her, the appellant

was only eager to set his record right; she further deposed that

the offer for reunion was only to save his face and without any

bonafides. It is also deposed that the appellant was not interested

in her and the children. She reiterated that the appellant was at

fault owing to his own conduct and life style. Her case was that

the appellant neglected her and children. Ext.B1 is the reply

notice to Ext.A1 lawyer notice. In that the respondent narrated

the attitude, conduct and character of the appellant.

7. The Family Court on an appreciation of pleadings and

evidence came to the conclusion that it is the appellant who had

deserted the respondent. It was specifically observed that the

appellant failed to "conquer the hearts of respondents and minor

children by love and affection." It was also noted that the

appellant failed to give support, respect and recognition to the
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:9:-

wife and; the appellant failed both as husband to his wife and

father for his children.

8. 'Desertion' as a ground for dissolution of marriage

under the Divorce Act is referred in Section 10(1)(ix) which

reads thus:

(ix) has deserted the petitioner for at least two years immediately preceding the

presentation of the petition;

9. Desertion, as referred under the Divorce Act though

is similar to the ground under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 ,

there is no statutory backing to the opposite party to plead and

prove, reasonable cause as a cause for separation as contained in

the explanation in the ground of desertion mentioned under

 Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act.

10. 'Desertion' is defined in the Halsbury's Law of England

[5th Edn. Vol 72 (2009)] as follows:

MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:10:-

In its essence desertion means the intentional, permanent forsaking and

abandonment of one party by the other without that other's consent, and

without reasonable cause. It is a total repudiation of one party's obligations.

11. In Black's Law Dictionary, desertion is defined as "the

willful and unjustified abandonment of a person's duties or

obligations, esp. to military service or to a spouse or a family".

12. In Bipinchandra Jaisinghbai Shah v. Prabhavati [AIR

1957 SC 176] under the Bombay Hindu Divorce Act, 1947, the

Apex Court referred to two essential conditions for desertion,

namely, (i) the factum of separation and (2) the intention to

bring cohabitation permanently to an end.

13. In Pulford v. Pulford [(1922) All E.R. Rep. 121],

'desertion' is defined as abandonment and withdrawal from

cohabitation. It is appropriate to refer the relevant statement on

the point of law in the judgment, which is as follows:

The statement of Lord Penzance that "Desertion means abandonment, and

implies an active withdrawal from a cohabitation that exists" (L. R. 1 P. & M.
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:11:-

697), is not an exhaustive definition of desertion. The conduct of the party

charged must be looked at. If he or she has not recognized the duty of

cohabitation in the married state, desertion has arisen. There may be a complete

renunciation of that conjugal duty and an intention to put an end to

cohabitation, though there is no matrimonial home, and cohabitation as an

existing state of things has been suspended by circumstances not under the

control of the party.

14. Similarly in Hopes v. Hopes [(1948) 2 ALL E.R. 920,

CA], it is interesting to refer the remarks of Lord Denning on

desertion. Lord Denning posed a question whether desertion

exist while the parties are living under the same roof? The

answer was "Yes". According to Lord Denning, when a spouse

himself or herself shuts up in one or two rooms in the same

house and have nothing to do with the other spouse and living

separately, effectively, desertion would exist. According to Lord

Denning, if the spouse had forsaken and abandoned

cohabitation, a case of desertion would be attracted.
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:12:-

15. The Division Bench of this Court in

P.C.Kunhinarayanan v. Vijayakumari [2021 (3) KLJ 906] held

that when the spouse refuses offer to cohabit without reasonable

cause it amounts to desertion.

16. In Rayden on Divorce [Vol.1, Edn.14, Pg.249] after

referring to various case laws discussed meaning of 'desertion' as

follows:

Meaning of desertion. The Court has discouraged attempts at defining

desertion, there being no general principle applicable to all cases. In its essence

desertion is the separation of one spouse from the other, with an intention on

the part of the deserting spouse of bringing cohabitation permanently to an end

without reasonable cause and without the consent of the other spouse; but the

physical act of departure by one spouse does not necessarily make that spouse

the deserting party. Desertion is not a withdrawal from a place, but from a state

of things, for what the law seeks to enforce is the recognition and discharge of

the common obligations of the married state; the state of things may be termed,

for short, 'the home'. There can be desertion without previous cohabitation by

the parties, or without the marriage having been consummated. The fact that a
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:13:-

husband makes an allowance to a wife he has abandoned is no answer to a

charge of desertion. Consensual divorce is now permitted, but consent to

separation is not the same as consent to divorce, and, as stated, where the

separation is consensual there is no desertion.

17. In understanding desertion, the Court first has to

examine who left the matrimonial home and secondly, the

spouse who left has any intention to return to the matrimonial

home and resume cohabitation. The desertion begins when the

spouse declares not to resume cohabitation after leaving

matrimonial home. Spouse may have reasons or dislikes to

cohabit with the other spouse. If that reason or cohabitation

reached to a point in declaring not to resume cohabitation, the

Court has to hold that desertion commenced from that stage.

18. In the absence of any stipulation allowing a spouse

who separated to plead and prove reasonable cause in a like

manner under the Hindu Marriage Act , this Court has to

examine how a 'separation' will constitute 'desertion' under the
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:14:-
 Divorce Act . There may be circumstances where a spouse is

forced to separate on account of cruelty, misbehaviour,

adulterous behaviour of other spouse and any other like causes.

If the spouse is forced to live separately, the Court cannot hold

that such spouse has deserted the petitioner who is seeking

divorce on the ground of desertion. The recognition of desertion

as a ground for divorce is based on the fault theory of divorce.

The fault theory presupposes that the opposite party in a petition

for divorce had committed a matrimonial guilt and the petitioner

is an innocent party. If the petitioner is at fault and the opposite

party is innocent, the Court cannot allow such petition to grant

divorce. Therefore, the Court has to examine the factual scenario

that resulted in separation. It is also to be noted that the opposite

party in a petition for divorce initiated under the Divorce Act 

has no statutorily recognized right to show reasonable cause for

such separation. However, the Court cannot withhold it from
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:15:-

examining the fault aspect related to grant of divorce. The Court

can grant divorce only in a circumstance on being satisfied that

the opposite party is at fault and the petitioner is innocent in

relation to the ground canvassed for divorce.

19. In this case, it is clear from the pleadings as well as

the evidence adduced on the side of the respondent that she has

no intention to resume cohabitation with the appellant. It also

has come out in evidence adduced by the appellant that he made

attempt to resume cohabitation. The oral testimony of PW2 and

PW3 cannot be overlooked in order to prove the attempt made

by the appellant to resume cohabitation. The evidence shows

that the appellant had no intention to abandon or separate the

marriage. The problem appears to be inherent incompatibility of

the parties. Ext.A3 report of the Consultant Psychiatrist and

Ext.A4 of the private Mediator vouchsafe that there exist lack of

emotional intimacy between the parties. The life style of the
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:16:-

appellant is attributed as the cause for separation by the

respondent-wife. However, it is to be noted that the respondent

failed to prove or substantiate any case of forced separation. If

the emotional intimacy is not built in a marriage, such marriage

is bound to collapse. If the ways of life of a partner is disliked by

the opposite partner, one cannot force the other partner to lead a

life of his/her choice. The outlook and approach may vary and

differ. It differs from person to person. To sustain a meaningful

marriage life, compromise is essential. If one tries to exert

control over other, it escalates to differences and disputes.

Learning to respect each other is the key in a healthy marital

relationship. If one expects the other to follow the way of life

he/she wants, it is for the other spouse to decide to follow or not

to follow. If both cannot find ways and means to lead a sustained

marital life, it would be ideal for them to part. A spouse cannot

demand the other spouse to follow his/her life style, and if that
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:17:-

becomes cause of rift for separation, fault becomes prominent on

the part of a spouse who separates. In this case what looms large

is that the appellant's life style caused discomfort to the

respondent-wife. The appellant-husband is not prepared to

change or mend his lifestyle in a way the respondent-wife

wants. It looks like that the respondent does not like the flashy

life style of appellant husband. According to her, the appellant,

instead of showing understanding of the matrimonial

relationship in a manner she perceived, behaved obnoxiously.

She appears to be a person more interested in having a private

life with her husband and children and not beyond. We find

nothing wrong with the such an attitude of the respondent but

that cannot be forced upon the appellant. The separation of the

respondent, therefore, has to be understood as if it was her

choice and not forced by the appellant-husband. If that be so,

desertion begun from the moment she opted for such choice. The
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 434 OF 2016
 -:18:-

choice so opted thus becomes her fault in a context of

matrimonial relationship to enable husband to obtain divorce.

Thus, the meaning of desertion in such context also includes

cessation or withdrawal from cohabitation. We, in such a

situation deem it appropriate to hold that the respondent had no

intention to resume cohabitation which resulted in desertion of

the appellant. We allow this appeal. The impugned judgment is

set aside. The decree of divorce is granted by dissolving the

marriage solemnized between the appellant and the respondent

on 26.12.1994. No costs.
Sd/-

A.MUHAMED MUSTAQUE, JUDGE

 Sd/-

DR.KAUSER EDAPPAGATH,JUDGE
